summary_paragraph: A middle-aged woman with type 1 diabetes, a history of two kidney transplants, and hypothyroidism was admitted for evaluation of atypical chest pain. She reported intermittent chest pressure radiating to the shoulder, associated with one episode of vomiting. Initial workup, including serial troponins and an exercise stress test, showed no evidence of acute myocardial infarction. The chest pain was ultimately deemed likely musculoskeletal. During the hospitalization, she was found to have a urinary tract infection caused by ciprofloxacin-resistant E. coli, confirmed by urine culture. She was treated with oral Macrobid, with resolution of fever and symptoms. Her immunosuppressive regimen was adjusted: cyclosporine was discontinued, and sirolimus dosing was modified. Her levothyroxine dose was reduced due to a low TSH level. Blood glucose levels were elevated, attributed to the infectious state, and managed in coordination with the diabetes team. She remained stable throughout her stay and was discharged home on a revised medication regimen with follow-up instructions.
